title: Probably Approximately Correct Labels
claim: Thresholding on uncertainty with a high-probability error upper bound meets a target error: use AI labels below the threshold and expert labels above.
layout: 1 plot, left-to-right axes, dashed target line, arrows splitting AI vs expert labels
description: A single schematic line plot. The x-axis is the uncertainty threshold u and the y-axis is labeling error. Two rising, S-shaped curves start near the origin. The dark-blue upper curve is labeled as the upper bound L-hat^u(alpha). The lighter-blue curve below it is the true error L^u. A horizontal red dashed line marks the target error epsilon. It meets the upper bound curve at a vertical dashed red line down to u-hat on the x-axis. A fainter dashed line drops from the true-error curve to u*, slightly to the right. Below the axis, a bracket at u-hat has two arrows. The left arrow reads 'collect AI labels' and the right arrow reads 'collect expert labels'. The eye goes first to the two curves and the red dashed intersection.
caption: Illustration of PAC labeling. The procedure estimates an uncertainty threshold ˆu and collects expert labels for all points where Ui ≥ˆu.
abstract: Obtaining high-quality labeled datasets is often costly, requiring either human annotation or expensive experiments. In theory, powerful pre-trained AI models provide an opportunity to automatically label datasets and save costs. Unfortunately, these models come with no guarantees on their accuracy, making wholesale replacement of manual labeling impractical. In this work, we propose a method for leveraging pre-trained AI models to curate cost-effective and high-quality datasets. In particular, our approach results in probably approximately correct labels: with high probability, the overall labeling error is small. Our method is nonasymptotically valid under minimal assumptions on the dataset or the AI model being studied, and thus enables rigorous yet efficient dataset curation using modern AI models. We demonstrate the benefits of the methodology through text annotation with large language models, image labeling with pre-trained vision models, and protein folding analysis with AlphaFold.
